nodes.text: Mercury, born of Maia; now he is held a great
god, he whose expertise gave [the world] thieves;
and that same one, most learned in Thessalian magic,
is said, by the control of the wand he took up, to have recalled extinguished
souls into the light, and the Cocytean laws of death
to have unsealed, as the shades flew back upward,
but to have condemned others to death, and deep into hidden
chaos to have plunged them. So it comes about that he was skilled at both
and had armed his life with a twofold crime;
for to call up thin shapes with magic murmur,
and skilfully to enchant the ashes of the tomb,
and likewise to rob others of life, his harmful art knew [how].
Simple antiquity, marvelling at this craftsman of crimes,
worshipped him as more than human, imagining him borne through the clouds
and running across the light winds on winged feet.
Look! formed among the number of the gods, and in bronze, there stands
a Greek man, and he gleams in Numa's august citadel.
The first face of the road is rough, bristling, gloomy,
difficult, but at its end most beautiful, and endowed
with ample riches, and abounding in everlasting light,
and such as can repay the labours that are past.
On the manifold [way] a demon is at hand as guide, who on the left side
confounds a hundred-forked path; he drags from there sophists,
bearded ones; he drags from here men mighty in wealth or office;
he lures with the tongues of birds and cheats with the haruspex,
he goads with the riddling of the raving old Sibyl,
he entangles in astrology, drives into the magic arts,
tempts with omens, catches with the augur, terrifies with entrails.
You see how it is one road, straying with many windings,
having submitted to such a guide as would not let [men] go by [the way] of salvation
